case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Navajo Nation’s suit—seeking to compel the United States to assess, plan for, and secure water for the Nation—impermissibly functions as a de facto quantification or reallocation of Lower Colorado River Mainstream water rights that must be litigated (if at all) within the Supreme Court’s retained jurisdiction under Arizona v. California, and whether any enforceable federal trust duty supports such relief.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Primarily the federal common-law/contract-like framework governing enforceable Indian trust duties (as articulated in the Mitchell line of cases), and the Supreme Court’s retained jurisdiction and decree structure in Arizona v. California (interpreting and implementing the Boulder Canyon Project Act and the ‘Law of the River’ allocation regime for the Lower Colorado River).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (States/water users and the Department of the Interior) argue that, notwithstanding the Ninth Circuit’s ‘artful’ narrowing of the pleadings, the requested injunction would in substance require the United States to deliver or prioritize Mainstream water for the Navajo Nation, which necessarily entails quantifying or reallocating rights governed by the Arizona v. California Consolidated Decree; because the Supreme Court retained jurisdiction to administer and adjust that decree, lower-court adjudication would intrude on (and potentially conflict with) the decree and the Supreme Court’s continuing supervisory role. They further argue that the Nation cannot obtain mandatory relief absent a specific, rights-creating source of law that ‘expressly’ imposes fiduciary obligations to identify, plan for, and secure water—general statements of the trust relationship, policy documents, or non-binding orders (e.g., the Krulitz Memo; Secretarial Order 3335 disclaimers) do not create enforceable duties.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the Navajo Nation) contend that the amended complaint is not a claim to adjudicate, quantify, or take a share of Lower Colorado River Mainstream rights under the Arizona decree; instead it seeks to enforce the federal government’s trust responsibilities by requiring Interior to evaluate the Nation’s water needs and to take planning/administrative steps within its existing authority without modifying the Arizona v. California decree. They also invoke the federal-tribal trust relationship and related federal statutes/regulations/executive actions as creating (or at least supporting) enforceable duties sufficient to survive dismissal and allow the trust claim to proceed, and they argue that retained jurisdiction in Arizona v. California does not automatically make Supreme Court jurisdiction exclusive for any case that touches on Colorado River management.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “planning-only” approach is the best effort to avoid Arizona v. California, but I remain unpersuaded that a court can enjoin Interior to “assess, plan for, and secure” water without effectively compelling identification and prioritization of Mainstream supplies—creating a substantial risk of conflicting directives with the Consolidated Decree and this Court’s retained jurisdiction. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Mitchell II and our Navajo Nation cases require a specific, administrable, duty-imposing source of law before we authorize mandatory injunctive relief compelling affirmative executive action; the cited treaty homeland/agriculture promises and generalized trust principles do not supply that clear hook. Judicial minimalism and institutional legitimacy counsel resolving narrowly on those grounds—no broad pronouncements about Winters rights, just an insistence on a concrete legal duty and avoidance of collateral lower-court supervision over the Law of the River. I therefore maintain my vote to reverse and direct dismissal (or leave any allocation disputes to the decree framework).
